cards.title: Understanding React's Rendering Engine
cards.content:
To optimize a React application, you must first understand how rendering works. React updates the UI in two main steps:

  • Render Phase: React calls your components to determine what needs to be changed in the Virtual DOM.
  • Commit Phase: React applies those changes to the actual browser DOM.

Performance bottlenecks usually happen when unnecessary renders are triggered repeatedly down the component tree.

cards.title: Skipping Renders with React.memo
cards.content:
By default, when a parent component re-renders, all of its child components re-render as well, regardless of whether their props changed.

React.memo is a higher-order component that shallowly compares props and skips re-rendering the child if props have not changed.

const MyComponent = React.memo(function MyComponent(props) {
  return <div>{props.value}</div>;
});

content.question: What kind of comparison does React.memo perform on props by default?

options.text: Shallow comparison (referential equality for objects, value equality for primitives)
No comparison; it always skips re-rendering
Strict equality comparison of the entire component function signature

cards.title: useMemo vs useCallback
cards.content:
When passing objects, arrays, or functions as props, React.memo can fail because those values get re-created on every render, changing their reference.

  • useMemo: Caches the *result* of a calculation.
  • useCallback: Caches the *function definition* itself.
// Memoizing a value
const dynamicValue = useMemo(() => computeExpensiveValue(a), [a]);

// Memoizing a function
const handleClick = useCallback(() => {
  doSomething(b);
}, [b]);

content.text: To prevent a child component from re-rendering because of a callback prop, you should wrap the handler function in the [blank] hook before passing it down.

cards.title: Code Splitting with React.lazy
cards.content:
Large bundle sizes slow down the initial load time of your application. React allows you to split your bundle and load components on-demand using React.lazy and Suspense.

import React, { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';

const HeavyComponent = lazy(() => import('./HeavyComponent'));

function App() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
      <HeavyComponent />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

pairs.right: Skips re-rendering a component if its props haven't changed
Caches the computed result of an expensive calculation
Caches a function instance to maintain referential identity
Dynamically imports components to reduce initial bundle size

cards.title: Rendering Large Lists: Virtualization
cards.content:
If you render thousands of items in a list, the browser DOM will struggle to handle so many elements. This causes lagging and slow UI updates.

List Virtualization solves this by rendering only the items currently visible in the user's viewport (plus a tiny buffer). As the user scrolls, old items are destroyed and new items are mounted dynamically.

Popular libraries for this include react-window and react-virtualized.

cards.title: Order the React Rendering Lifecycle Steps

content.instruction: Arrange the steps of the React update cycle in chronological order from state trigger to execution of side effects.

items.text: A state change is triggered via a setter function (e.g., setState).
React executes the component functions and runs the diffing algorithm (Render Phase).
React writes the changes to the real DOM (Commit Phase).
The browser paints the screen and the useEffect hooks run asynchronously.
